Money and network that has run since January 2009 with no company, government or central bank behind it. Anyone can use it without asking permission, and anyone can check the rules. For a bitcoiner it means money nobody can print at will, freeze or confiscate if you hold your own keys: a way to save and pay that depends on math and on thousands of people verifying, not on trusting a middleman.

Two things at once: the first name of Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, and the smallest unit of bitcoin, one hundred-millionth of a coin. Naming the unit after Satoshi is a quiet tribute. It also matters in practice: since one bitcoin splits into 100,000,000 sats, anyone can own a piece, even with a few coins in their pocket.

Plural of satoshi, the smallest unit of bitcoin. Bitcoiners often think and count in sats instead of whole coins, because that's how most people actually save: a few thousand at a time. Lightning payments are usually priced in sats, and 'stacking sats' is the habit of putting a little aside regularly in money that can't be inflated away.

Surname in the pseudonym of Bitcoin's creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, who wrote the whitepaper, released the first software and then stepped away around 2011 without ever revealing who they were. Bitcoiners see that disappearance as a gift: with no founder to arrest, pressure or follow, Bitcoin has no leader, only rules that everyone can verify.

Bundle of transactions that a miner adds to the timechain about every ten minutes. Each block includes the hash of the previous one, so they're chained together and rewriting the past would mean redoing all the work since then. Block space is limited on purpose, which keeps nodes cheap to run, so transactions compete with fees to get in.

What blocks form when each one points to the hash of the one before. Nodes follow the valid chain with the most accumulated proof of work. If someone tried to alter an old transaction, every link after it would break and they'd have to redo all that energy. That's why the history of bitcoin is so hard to rewrite.

Word the rest of the world uses for what bitcoiners prefer to call the timechain: the public, linked record of every Bitcoin transaction. Satoshi wrote about a chain of blocks but never used it as one word. Bitcoiners are wary of the buzzword because, without proof of work and open verification, a 'blockchain' is often just a slow database with an owner.

Person or company that runs specialized machines to find the next block. Miners pick transactions from the mempool, order them and spend real energy searching for a valid hash; in return they earn the subsidy plus fees. That cost is the point: it makes attacking the timechain extremely expensive, and no miner can change the rules that nodes enforce.

Process of securing Bitcoin with proof of work: machines try trillions of hashes until one meets the difficulty target and seals a block. It turns electricity into security, issues new coins on a fixed schedule and gives the timechain an order nobody can fake. It's also open to anyone, with no permission needed to join.

Computer running Bitcoin software that downloads the timechain and checks every block and transaction against the rules on its own. Running one is how you stop trusting and start verifying: your node won't accept extra coins or invalid spends, no matter who sends them. Thousands of independent nodes are what really defend the rules.

Moment every 210,000 blocks, roughly every four years, when the new coins miners get per block are cut in half. It started at 50 BTC; after the 2024 halving it's 3.125. It's written into the code and no one can skip or delay it. For bitcoiners it's the heartbeat of a predictable, ever-scarcer supply, the opposite of money printed on demand.

Fixed-length fingerprint a cryptographic function produces from any data. Change a single comma and the result is completely different, and you can't work backwards from it. Bitcoin uses SHA-256 hashes everywhere: to link blocks, identify transactions and run proof of work. It's what makes the record tamper-evident for anyone who checks.

Number a miner keeps changing in the block header, again and again, hoping the resulting hash comes out below the target. The name means 'number used once'. It's the heart of the mining lottery: there's no shortcut, only trying, which is why a valid block is honest proof that real work was done.

Software or device that manages your keys. It doesn't actually hold coins, which live on the timechain; it holds what lets you move them. Hot wallets are online and convenient, cold ones stay offline and safer. The wallet a bitcoiner cares about is one where they hold the keys, because that's what self-custody means.

List of 12 or 24 words, from the BIP39 list, that backs up all the keys of a wallet. With it you can rebuild your funds on any compatible wallet, even if your device breaks; without it, a lost device can mean lost bitcoin. It's best written on paper or steel and kept offline, because whoever has those words has your money.

Secret number, the private key, that lets you sign and spend your bitcoin, paired with a public key used to receive. Whoever controls the private key controls the coins, which is why bitcoiners say 'not your keys, not your coins'. Holding your own keys is what turns bitcoin into money nobody can freeze for you.

Cryptographic proof that the owner of a private key authorized a transaction, made without revealing the key. Anyone can check it with the public key, so no bank needs to vouch for you. Bitcoin uses ECDSA and, since Taproot, Schnorr signatures. Signatures are what make spending permissionless and forgery practically impossible.

Waiting room where unconfirmed transactions sit until a miner puts them in a block. There isn't one single mempool: each node keeps its own. When it fills up, people outbid each other with higher fees and cheap transactions wait longer. Watching it tells you how busy the network is and how much to pay.

Payment network built on top of Bitcoin, a layer two. Users open channels and send sats back and forth instantly with tiny fees, settling on the timechain only when they open or close. It lets bitcoin work for everyday payments, like a coffee or a tip, without filling blocks, and you can keep your own keys while doing it.

In Lightning, a shared balance two nodes lock in an on-chain transaction so they can pay each other off-chain as many times as they want. Only opening and closing touch the timechain. Linked channels let payments hop across the network to almost anyone, which is how Lightning scales Bitcoin without giving up custody.

Soft fork activated in November 2021 that brought Schnorr signatures and a smarter way to hide spending conditions. Complex setups, like multisig or contracts, can look like ordinary payments, revealing only the path actually used. It improved privacy and efficiency, and it was adopted without splitting the network.

Short for Segregated Witness, the soft fork activated in 2017 that moved signature data into a separate part of the transaction. It fixed transaction malleability, which made Lightning practical, and added more room per block without a hard fork. Its activation was a hard fight that showed that users running nodes, not big companies, decide the rules.

Signature scheme named after cryptographer Claus Schnorr, added to Bitcoin with Taproot. Schnorr signatures are simple, compact and can be combined, so several signers can produce what looks like a single signature. That saves block space and improves privacy, since a shared wallet can look just like anyone else's.

Name of Ralph Merkle, a public-key cryptography pioneer, and of the Merkle tree: a structure that hashes transactions in pairs up to a single root stored in the block header. It lets a light wallet prove a transaction is in a block without downloading it all, and makes any tampering with a block's contents obvious.

First block of the timechain, mined by Satoshi on January 3, 2009. It's the only block that points to no previous one, and its coinbase carries a headline from The Times about a bank bailout, a timestamp and a statement of why Bitcoin exists. Its 50-bitcoin reward can't be spent.

Measure of how hard it is to find a valid block. Every 2016 blocks, about two weeks, the network adjusts it automatically: if more hashpower joined, it rises; if miners leave, it drops. That keeps blocks coming roughly every ten minutes and keeps issuance on schedule, no matter how many machines are mining.

New bitcoin a miner earns for each block, created out of nothing in the coinbase transaction. It began at 50 BTC and halves every 210,000 blocks; today it's 3.125. It's how all bitcoin entered circulation, on a public schedule. As it shrinks, miners will rely more and more on fees to keep the network secure.

What you pay a miner to include your transaction in a block. It depends on how many bytes the transaction takes, measured in sats per vbyte, not on the amount you send: moving a fortune can cost the same as moving a little. Fees are also the long-term security budget of Bitcoin, once the subsidy fades.

Unspent transaction output: a chunk of bitcoin locked to someone and not yet spent. Bitcoin has no accounts with balances; your wallet adds up your UTXOs. To pay, it spends some whole and sends the change back to you. Understanding them helps with fees and privacy, since combining UTXOs can link your history.

Transaction ID: the hash that uniquely identifies each Bitcoin transaction. You can look it up in a block explorer, or better yet in your own node, to see whether a payment confirmed and in which block. It's the receipt nobody can fake, because anyone can check it against the timechain.

Quality of something limited that can't be easily produced. Bitcoin's scarcity is absolute: never more than 21 million, enforced by every node and immune to any government's or company's decisions. Gold is scarce because it's hard to mine; bitcoin is scarce because the rules say so and everyone can verify them.

Agreement among thousands of independent nodes on which transactions and blocks are valid, without anyone in charge. Each node enforces the same rules, and proof of work settles which valid chain to follow. Changing the rules needs broad agreement from users, which is what protects Bitcoin from capture by miners, companies or governments.

Rule change that tightens the rules in a backward-compatible way: old nodes still accept the new blocks, so the network doesn't split. SegWit and Taproot arrived this way. Bitcoiners prefer soft forks because they let the protocol improve carefully, without forcing anyone to upgrade to keep using their money.

Rule change that isn't backward-compatible: nodes that don't upgrade reject the new blocks, so the network can split in two. That's how Bitcoin Cash broke off in 2017. Bitcoin has avoided them because they'd force everyone to switch, and the original rules kept the support of users who run their own nodes.

Science of protecting information with math. Bitcoin rests on it: hashes link blocks and power mining, and digital signatures prove ownership without revealing your private key. Thanks to cryptography, you don't need to trust anyone with your money, only the math, which anyone can check.

Ability to decide what you show about yourself and to whom. The Cypherpunk Manifesto called it necessary for an open society. Bitcoin is public, so every transaction can be seen; protecting privacy takes care: new addresses, CoinJoin, Lightning, your own node. It's not about hiding wrongdoing, it's about not exposing your whole financial life.

Activist who defends privacy and freedom with cryptography and code instead of asking permission. In the 1990s they shared ideas on a mailing list, and many precursors of Bitcoin came from that world. Satoshi published the whitepaper on a related cryptography list. Their motto, roughly, is 'cypherpunks write code'.

Nine-page paper Satoshi Nakamoto published on October 31, 2008, titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System'. It explains how to prevent double spending without a trusted third party, using proof of work and a public chain of blocks. Bitcoiners keep going back to it, because the core ideas are all there.

Word born from a typo in a 2013 forum post titled 'I AM HODLING', written by someone who refused to sell in a price drop. It became a philosophy: hold your bitcoin long term and ignore the noise. Later people read it as 'Hold On for Dear Life'. Behind the joke there's a serious idea: saving in money that can't be inflated.

Who holds the keys to the bitcoin. If an exchange or app holds them, you have a promise from them, not bitcoin, and they can freeze it, lose it or go bust. Self-custody means holding your own keys, with the responsibility of backing them up. For bitcoiners it's the step that makes the coins really yours.

Setup where spending requires several signatures out of a group of keys, for example two of three. It removes the single point of failure: a lost or stolen key doesn't mean lost funds. It's useful for families, companies and inheritance plans, and lets you share control without handing custody to a third party.

Protocol that lets several signers combine their Schnorr signatures into one, so a shared wallet looks like a single-key wallet on the timechain. It saves block space and fees and improves privacy, since nobody can tell several people agreed. MuSig2 is the version most used today.

Extended public key: from it a wallet can derive all your receiving addresses, but it can't spend. You can load it into a watch-only app to see your balance while the private keys stay on your hardware wallet. Treat it with care anyway: whoever has it can see your whole history.

Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction: a standard format for passing a transaction between wallets and devices until it has all the signatures it needs. It's what makes it easy to sign with an offline hardware wallet or to coordinate a multisig among several people, without exposing any private key.

String you share so someone can send you bitcoin; it's derived from your public key. Modern ones start with bc1. It's best to use a new one for every payment, because reusing addresses lets anyone link your payments together. Giving out an address never puts your funds at risk.

Practice network that works just like Bitcoin, but its coins are worthless on purpose. Developers test software there and newcomers can learn to use wallets without risking real money. Its coins are handed out free by faucets. A good place to make mistakes before doing it for real.

Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip built to do just one thing, in Bitcoin's case compute SHA-256 hashes for mining. ASICs replaced graphics cards and made mining a serious industry. Their hashpower is what makes attacking the timechain so expensive.

Group of miners who combine their hashpower and share the rewards in proportion to the work each contributes. It gives small miners a steady income instead of waiting years for a lucky block. Bitcoiners keep an eye on pool concentration and support protocols that let miners build their own blocks.

Each block added on top of the block that includes your transaction. One confirmation means it's in the timechain; each new one makes reversing it harder. Six is a common rule of thumb for large amounts, and zero means it's still in the mempool. It's how you know a payment is settled without asking anyone.

What proof of work turns into security. Mining spends real electricity, so rewriting the timechain would cost an enormous amount of it. Miners hunt for the cheapest power, which often means energy that would otherwise be wasted, so Bitcoin ties digital money to something physical that can't be faked.

Loss of money's purchasing power, usually because more of it is created. Argentines know it well: savings in pesos melt away over time. Bitcoin's issuance is fixed and capped at 21 million, so no one can dilute your savings by printing. That's one of the main reasons people adopt it.

Money by decree: pesos, dollars or euros, worth something because a government says so and requires it, not because it's scarce. Its supply depends on political decisions, so it tends to lose value. Bitcoin offers the alternative: money whose rules nobody can change at will.

Metal that served as money for thousands of years because it's scarce, durable and hard to produce. Bitcoin is often called digital gold, since it shares those traits and adds others: it's easy to divide, cheap to verify and can cross a border in your head. You can't print either one.

Tool for exchanging, measuring value and saving across time. For bitcoiners, good money must be scarce, portable, divisible and hard to censor; Bitcoin aims to be the soundest money ever made, and the first that works without a state behind it.

Power to decide for yourself. In Bitcoin, financial sovereignty means holding your own keys and running your own node: nobody can freeze your funds, block your payments or change the rules on you. It's what being your own bank means, with the responsibility that comes with it.

Hal Finney, cryptographer and veteran cypherpunk who was one of the first to run Bitcoin. He received the first Bitcoin transaction from Satoshi in January 2009, tweeted 'Running bitcoin' and helped find and fix bugs in the early software. Bitcoiners remember him as a key early supporter.

Nick Szabo, computer scientist and legal scholar who coined the term 'smart contract' and designed Bit Gold, a proposal for scarce digital money based on proof of work. Many ideas in Bitcoin echo his work, and his essays on money and trust are still widely read by bitcoiners.

Proof-of-work system Adam Back proposed in 1997 to fight spam: each email needed a small computational effort, cheap for one but costly in bulk. The Bitcoin whitepaper cites it, and mining uses the same idea to make blocks costly to produce and the timechain hard to rewrite.

Proposal by Nick Szabo for decentralized digital money that combined proof of work, timestamps and unforgeable scarcity. It was never built, but it anticipated many ideas that Bitcoin brought to life, which is why bitcoiners see it as one of its direct ancestors.

On May 22, 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, one of the first known purchases of real goods with bitcoin. Each year bitcoiners celebrate Bitcoin Pizza Day, not to mourn the price but to honor the moment bitcoin proved it could work as money.

Programmer Laszlo Hanyecz, famous for buying two pizzas with 10,000 BTC in May 2010, the origin of Bitcoin Pizza Day. He also contributed code and is credited as a pioneer of mining with graphics cards. His purchase showed that bitcoin could be used to pay for real things.

Open protocol for publishing signed notes through independent relays, used mostly as a social network with no owner. Your identity is a key pair, so no company can ban you or take your account. It was created by the developer known as fiatjaf, Jack Dorsey backed it with donations, and many bitcoiners use it with Lightning tips built in.

Small Lightning payment in sats sent to a post or a person, common on Nostr. It's like a 'like' that carries real value and goes straight to the author, with no platform in between. Zaps show what Lightning makes possible: tiny, instant payments to anyone in the world.

Transaction where several people combine their coins, each paying themselves equal-looking amounts, so it's hard to tell who owns which output. Nobody hands over custody: each participant signs only their part. It's a tool to recover privacy on a public timechain, and with it, the fungibility of bitcoin.

Transaction where both the payer and the receiver add inputs. It breaks the usual assumption that all inputs belong to the same person, which confuses chain analysis. It looks like a normal payment, so it improves privacy for everyone, even those who don't use it.

Simple, stack-based programming language that sets the conditions for spending each output: a signature, several signatures, a waiting time, a secret. It's deliberately limited, with no loops, to keep validation predictable and safe. Lightning, multisig and timelocks are all built with it.

Condition in a script that prevents spending until a certain date or block height. It's the basis of payment channels like Lightning and of inheritance setups where a backup key only works after some time. It lets you program money without trusting anyone to hold it.

Business where you buy and sell bitcoin, usually trading it for pesos, dollars or other money. It's often the way in, but leaving funds there means trusting them: they can freeze, lose or block your coins. Bitcoiners recommend buying and then withdrawing to your own wallet.

Know Your Customer: identity checks that exchanges and banks require, with your ID, a selfie and sometimes proof of address. It links your name to your bitcoin and leaves that data stored by third parties who can leak it. That's why many bitcoiners value buying peer to peer or without KYC when it's legal.

Optional extra word or phrase added to a seed, sometimes called the 25th word. With it, the same seed opens a completely different wallet, so if someone finds your words they still can't spend. The catch: if you forget it, nobody can recover it, not even with the seed.

Service that watches your Lightning channels while you're offline. If the other side tries to close the channel with an old, more favorable balance, the watchtower publishes the penalty transaction and you keep the funds. It helps you run Lightning without having to be online all the time.

Square code of black and white dots that a camera reads in a second. In Bitcoin it holds an address or a Lightning invoice, so you can pay by pointing your phone instead of typing long strings. It reduces mistakes and makes paying with bitcoin as easy as any app.

Separate chain where bitcoin can move through a peg, gaining features like faster blocks or confidential transactions. It lets people experiment without changing Bitcoin itself. Liquid and Rootstock are examples. The trade-off is trust: in today's sidechains, someone else guards the bitcoin while it's there.

Sidechain developed by Blockstream, run by a federation of members that produces one-minute blocks and guards the peg. Its L-BTC, backed by bitcoin, moves fast and with confidential amounts, which is handy for traders. Bitcoiners note the trade-off: you trust the federation.

Scheme created by Casey Rodarmor that numbers every satoshi to track individual sats and attach data like images, called inscriptions. It filled blocks and raised fees, and sparked a heated debate among bitcoiners about using block space for things that aren't money.

Proof that some data existed at a given moment. The whitepaper describes Bitcoin as a distributed timestamp server: each block seals transactions in an order nobody can change later. That's why bitcoiners call it the timechain, a clock and a record nobody controls.

Book of accounts that records who owns what. Bitcoin's is public and shared: every node keeps a full copy of the timechain and can audit it, so no bank or government holds the master copy. It's also the name of a hardware wallet brand.

What Bitcoin replaces with verification. Satoshi wrote that central banks must be trusted not to debase the currency, and history shows they often have. Bitcoin removes that need: instead of trusting a bank or a government, you check the rules yourself. Hence the motto 'don't trust, verify'.

To check for yourself instead of believing someone. 'Don't trust, verify' is the core of Bitcoin: your node verifies every block, every signature and the total supply. You don't need anyone's word. That's what gives you real control over your money and protects the rules.

Creation of new bitcoin, which follows a fixed and public schedule: miners get a subsidy that halves every 210,000 blocks, so it will end around the year 2140, with 21 million in total. Unlike money issued by central banks, nobody can speed it up, and everyone knows today how much there will be tomorrow.

Bitcoin's supply cap is 21 million coins, and there will never be more. That limit is enforced by every node and can't be changed without users accepting it. It's the number bitcoiners know by heart, because it sums up what makes Bitcoin unique: predictable, absolute scarcity.

Institutions that keep, lend and move money, and that depend on trust. The genesis block quotes a headline about a second bailout for UK banks during the 2008 crisis. Bitcoin was born as an alternative: money you can hold and send without asking any bank for permission.

British newspaper whose headline Satoshi embedded in the genesis block: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'. It proves the block wasn't mined before that day and leaves a message about why Bitcoin exists: an answer to bailouts and printed money.

In the UK, the minister in charge of finances. The headline in the genesis block mentions him: a chancellor on the brink of a second bank bailout. Satoshi left it there as a reminder of the system Bitcoin offers an alternative to, where governments rescue banks at savers' expense.

Rescue of companies, usually banks, with public money or newly printed money. The genesis block quotes a headline about a second one in 2009. Bailouts reward failure and the cost falls on everyone through debt or inflation. Bitcoin can't be bailed out: there's no one to print it.

Money you hand over directly, with no middleman, that settles on the spot. The whitepaper's title calls Bitcoin a 'peer-to-peer electronic cash system': the idea was to bring that same freedom of paper cash to the internet, without banks or permission.

Made of digital signals instead of paper or metal. The whitepaper calls Bitcoin an 'electronic cash system': money that lives on the internet but behaves like cash, passing directly from person to person, with no bank recording or approving each payment.

An equal. 'Peer-to-peer' is the architecture in the whitepaper's title: nodes connect directly to each other, with no central server that could be shut down. Each node is a peer with the same rights, which is why Bitcoin has no headquarters to raid or switch off.

Bitcoin Improvement Proposal: a public document where someone proposes a change or standard. Anyone can write one, and it's discussed openly. BIP39, for example, defines the seed words. Proposing doesn't mean imposing: a change only takes effect if users choose to run it.

A BIP39 seed is made of 12 or 24 words taken from an official list of 2048. Words are easier to write down and read back than long numbers, which reduces backup mistakes. Writing them down carefully, on paper or steel, is how you make sure you'll never lose your bitcoin.

Keeping keys on a device or on paper that never touches the internet is called cold storage: out of reach of hackers and malware. It is how bitcoiners store savings they won't spend soon, the opposite of a hot wallet used for daily payments.

Physical side of computing. A hardware wallet is a small device built only to keep keys and sign transactions offline: the private key never leaves it, even if your computer is infected. It's one of the most popular ways to do self-custody safely.

To accumulate sats bit by bit, buying regularly and keeping them. 'Stacking sats' is a bitcoiner habit: no rush, no trying to time the market, just saving in money that can't be printed. Over time, small amounts add up.

Dollar-cost averaging: buying the same amount at regular intervals, for example every week or month, regardless of the price. It removes the stress of guessing the right moment and evens out the swings. It's how many bitcoiners stack sats calmly, as a savings habit.

All-time high: the highest price ever reached. A new one makes headlines and brings newcomers, but bitcoiners know price is noise in the short term. What matters is what Bitcoin enables: savings that can't be inflated away and money nobody can confiscate.

Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt: news, rumors or claims meant to scare people about Bitcoin, like 'it's been banned' or 'it's dead'. Bitcoin has been declared dead many times and keeps producing blocks. The antidote is to understand how it works and verify for yourself.

What everyday bitcoiners call themselves: regular people, not whales or gurus, who stack sats, run nodes and help each other learn. In Bitcoin the plebs matter, because the users running nodes are the ones who enforce the rules and keep the network honest.

'Stay humble, stack sats' is a bitcoiner motto: keep accumulating calmly and don't get carried away when the price goes up, or panic when it falls. Humility also means knowing there's always more to learn about Bitcoin and that nobody can predict its price.

Time preference measures how much you value the present over the future. Money that loses value pushes people to spend now; scarce money like bitcoin rewards saving and long-term planning. That's why bitcoiners talk about 'lowering their time preference'.

Bitcoiners say 'tick tock, next block' to remind everyone that, whatever happens, a new block arrives about every ten minutes. Bitcoin keeps running on schedule, unbothered by news, crises or opinions, like a clock nobody can stop.

Short for Bitcoin maximalist: someone who thinks only Bitcoin is worth using as money and that other cryptocurrencies are a distraction or worse. Maxis argue that money tends toward the soundest option and that Bitcoin's decentralization and scarcity can't be copied.

Any cryptocurrency other than bitcoin. Many copy its code with changes and usually have a founder, a company or a pre-mined supply. Bitcoiners are skeptical: without Bitcoin's decentralization and fair launch, they say, the promised scarcity is just someone's promise.

Script opcode, written OP_RETURN, that marks an output as unspendable and lets it carry a small amount of data. It is used to anchor messages or proofs in the timechain without bloating the UTXO set that every node keeps. How much data it should allow is a recurring debate among bitcoiners.

Latin American Bitcoin & Blockchain Conference, born in Buenos Aires in 2013 and organized by people from Bitcoin Argentina. It has been held in cities across the region, bringing together developers, entrepreneurs and curious newcomers. For many Latin Americans it was their door into Bitcoin.

Total amount of a currency in existence. Bitcoin's is capped at 21 million and follows a public schedule, so it doesn't grow when demand rises or when someone needs money. Anyone with a node can check the exact supply at any moment, something no fiat currency allows.

How much and how fast a price moves. Bitcoin's is high because it's a young asset whose supply can't adjust to demand. It scares people who check the price daily; bitcoiners look at the long term and save what they won't need soon.

Able to be split into small parts. Each bitcoin divides into 100 million satoshis, so you can pay for a coffee or save a few pesos' worth. Divisibility lets a fixed supply of 21 million work as money for everyone.

Interchangeable: each unit is worth the same as any other. Good money must be fungible, but since Bitcoin's history is public, some try to 'taint' coins for where they've been. Protecting privacy with tools like CoinJoin helps keep every sat equal.

Able to be checked by anyone. Bitcoin's books are public: with your own node you can verify every transaction and confirm that there aren't more coins than the rules allow. No central bank offers that; in Bitcoin, nobody needs to take anyone's word.

Blocking or controlling what others can say or do, money included. Banks and governments can freeze accounts or stop transfers they dislike. Bitcoin was built to resist it: if your transaction pays a fair fee, some miner will include it, and no one can veto it. That is why we say Bitcoin is censorship-resistant money.

An authorization someone else has to grant you. With Bitcoin you don't need any: no one approves your wallet, your node or your payment, and no company decides who may join. Being permissionless means a teenager in Argentina and a bank in Zurich play by exactly the same rules.

The lines between countries, where money usually gets checked, taxed or stopped. Bitcoin doesn't see them: a transaction from Buenos Aires to Madrid is the same as one across the street. And if you memorize your seed, your savings can go with you anywhere, even if you leave with nothing else.

Inflated excitement, usually pushed by social media, that makes something look bigger than it is. Prices climb fast and then deflate, and people who bought on emotion get hurt. Bitcoiners learn to tune it out: what matters is understanding the money, keeping your own keys and thinking in years, not in candles.

Refers to quantum computing, which uses qubits instead of ordinary bits. A big enough quantum computer could in theory break the signatures Bitcoin uses today. That machine doesn't exist yet, and developers are already studying quantum-resistant signatures that could be added with a soft fork if needed. Worth watching, not panicking over.

A set of rules that computers follow to talk to each other. Bitcoin is an open protocol, not a company: there is no CEO and no headquarters, just rules that every node checks for itself. To change them you have to convince the people running nodes, which is what makes Bitcoin so hard to capture.

The instructions programmers write so a computer does something. Bitcoin's is open source: anyone can read it, compile it and check that it does what it promises. Some say 'code is law', but in Bitcoin the real law is the rules that thousands of node runners choose to run. Don't trust, verify.

A set of connected computers sharing information. Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer network: thousands of nodes around the world pass transactions and blocks to each other with no central server to shut down. Lightning is another network built on top of it for fast payments.

A signed message that moves bitcoin. It spends earlier outputs (inputs) and creates new ones (outputs), leaving a fee for the miner. You sign it with your private key, broadcast it to the network and wait for it to land in a block. No bank in the middle: just you, your keys and the rules.

The part of a transaction that spends an earlier output, a UTXO you control. Each input points to where the coins came from and carries the signature proving they are yours. Every node checks those signatures, so no one can spend coins that aren't theirs.

What a transaction creates: an amount of bitcoin locked to a condition, usually an address. Until it's spent it is a UTXO, and the sum of all UTXOs is the whole bitcoin supply. Your wallet balance is really a pile of outputs you can unlock with your keys.

The leftover that returns to you. Bitcoin outputs are spent whole, like bills: if you pay 30,000 sats with a 100,000-sat UTXO, your wallet creates a 70,000-sat output back to an address of yours, minus the fee. Good wallets send change to a fresh address to protect your privacy.

How much bitcoin you have available. There is no account holding a number: your wallet scans the timechain and adds up the unspent outputs your keys can open. If you run your own node, you check that sum yourself instead of trusting someone else's server.

Handing money to someone in exchange for something. In Bitcoin you pay directly, with no bank approving it. On-chain it settles in blocks; with Lightning it arrives in seconds and costs very little. Either way, no one can reverse it or freeze it along the way.

On Lightning, a payment request. It's a code starting with lnbc, often shown as a QR, that includes the amount, a description, an expiry and the hash of a secret. The payer's wallet reads it, finds a route and pays. It's how you ask to get paid without exposing your whole wallet.

The path a payment follows. On Lightning, if you have no direct channel with someone, your payment hops through other people's channels until it gets there. Your own node finds the route, and thanks to onion encryption, the nodes in between don't know who is paying whom.

In Lightning, how much money is available on each side of a channel. To send you need funds on your side; to receive you need inbound liquidity, room on the other side. Nodes rebalance channels so payments keep flowing. In markets, it means how easily you can buy or sell without moving the price.

One level built on top of another. Bitcoin is the base layer: slow on purpose, very secure and final. On top, second layers like Lightning handle fast, cheap payments while still relying on the base layer when it matters. This lets Bitcoin scale without giving up decentralization.

An open-source protocol where a group of guardians, for example trusted people in a community, jointly hold bitcoin in multisig and issue private ecash. No single guardian can run off with the funds. It's not full self-custody, but it's a big improvement on trusting one company, and it pays over Lightning.

Digital cash, based on David Chaum's blind signatures. A mint backed by sats issues tokens that work like bills: you spend them without the mint knowing who you are or what you bought. Cashu and Fedimint bring it to Bitcoin. You trust the mint with custody, but you gain privacy similar to paper money.

An open-source ecash protocol for Bitcoin, named after the cashew nut. A single mint holds the sats and issues blinded tokens that can travel as plain text, even in a chat message, and that settle over Lightning. You trust the mint with the funds, but it can't see who pays whom.

A spare copy kept in case something goes wrong. In Bitcoin the key backup is your seed phrase written down and stored safely. If your phone breaks or gets stolen, with the seed you get everything back; without it, the coins are lost forever. No company can recover them for you.

An alloy of iron and carbon, very hard. Bitcoiners use steel plates to engrave or stamp their seed phrase, because unlike paper they survive fire, flood and time. It's a cheap way to make sure your self-custody doesn't depend on a sheet of paper in a drawer.

In cryptography, the amount of randomness. A good seed needs a lot of it, so no one can guess your keys by trying. With 128 or 256 random bits, the possibilities are so many that no computer could go through them all. Low entropy, like a phrase you made up, makes your coins easy prey.

Cubes with six faces used to get random numbers. Some bitcoiners roll them to generate their own seed so they don't have to trust a device's randomness: each roll adds a bit over 2.5 bits of entropy, and 99 rolls give about 256. It's slow, but you verify it yourself.

A value computed from the data to catch mistakes. The last word of your seed includes one, so a wallet notices if you copied a word wrong. Addresses also carry one, so a typo doesn't send your sats into the void. A small detail that saves a lot of tears.

The way an HD wallet derives every key and address from your single seed, following a path like m/84'/0'/0'. That's why one backup covers everything. When restoring in another wallet, using the same derivation path matters: with a different one your coins seem to vanish, even though they are still there.

Something anyone can see. Your public key is derived from your private key and can be shared safely; addresses come from it. Everyone can check your signatures with it, but no one can work backward to the private key. The timechain is public too, so privacy takes some care.

Something that belongs only to you. Your private key is what signs transactions and therefore what truly owns your bitcoin. Whoever has it controls the coins; if you lose it or someone sees it, there's no one to call. That's why we say: not your keys, not your coins.

A line that isn't straight. Bitcoin's signatures rely on an elliptic curve called secp256k1: multiplying a point is easy, undoing it is practically impossible. That one-way math is what lets you prove the coins are yours without ever revealing your private key.

Someone who reveals what others can't see, like the one at Delphi. In Bitcoin, an outside source that reports a fact, such as a price or a match result, so a contract can settle. Designs like DLCs let the oracle sign the result without knowing who is betting or how much.

A strongly protected place for valuables. In Bitcoin, a setup that makes withdrawals wait for a delay, giving you time to cancel if a thief gets your keys. Today it's built with multisig and pre-signed transactions; proposals like OP_VAULT would make it simpler. It's about protecting self-custody, not handing it over.

A binding promise. In Bitcoin, a proposal to let coins restrict where they can go next, enabling vaults, cheaper channels and more. CTV and OP_VAULT are part of a long debate: some see useful tools, others fear too much control over money. Changes like this need broad agreement and get studied for years.

Short for reorganization: when nodes switch to a competing branch of the timechain with more accumulated work, dropping the latest blocks of the old one. Transactions in those blocks go back to the mempool. That's why big payments wait for several confirmations: the deeper a block, the harder it is to undo.

A child without parents. Bitcoiners use it for a valid block left out of the main chain because another miner found one at the same height and the other branch won. The losing miner loses the reward. Strictly speaking it's a stale block, but 'orphan' stuck.

The top part, like a letterhead. A block header is 80 bytes: previous block hash, Merkle root of the transactions, time, difficulty target and nonce. Miners hash it over and over looking for a valid result. With headers alone, even a light wallet can check how much work backs the chain.

How tall something is. In Bitcoin, the number of blocks since the genesis block: each new block adds one. Many things are tied to height, like halvings every 210,000 blocks; the fourth was at height 840,000. It's the timechain's own way of counting time.

An era or period. In Bitcoin, the 2016 blocks between difficulty adjustments, about two weeks if blocks come every ten minutes. At the end of each epoch the network looks at how long it took and adjusts difficulty, with no one in charge deciding it.

An automatic correction. Every 2016 blocks the network compares how long they took with the two weeks expected and raises or lowers the difficulty. If miners join, it gets harder; if they leave, easier. That keeps issuance on schedule and the supply predictable, no matter how much hashpower there is.

The total computing power miners put into Bitcoin, measured in hashes per second, today in exahashes. The higher it is, the more expensive it is to attack the network, because rewriting history would mean outdoing all that work. It's the energy wall protecting your sats.

The first transaction of every block, the one that pays the miner the subsidy plus fees. That's how new bitcoins are born. In the genesis block Satoshi left a headline there: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks'. It's also the name of an exchange, unrelated.

The center of something. Bitcoin Core is the most widely used node software, descended from Satoshi's original code, with hundreds of contributors over the years. It has no boss: changes go through public review, and each person chooses which version to run. Running your own node is how you verify instead of trusting.

Fastenings tied in rope, or a unit of speed at sea. In Bitcoin, Bitcoin Knots is a node implementation derived from Bitcoin Core and maintained by Luke Dashjr, with more options and stricter mempool policies. Having alternatives reminds us that each node runner chooses their own software.

A made-up name used instead of your real one. Satoshi Nakamoto is the most famous in Bitcoin, and their anonymity helped: there's no founder to pressure. Bitcoin itself is pseudonymous, not anonymous: addresses don't carry names, but everything is public, so if someone links an address to you, they can follow it.

Having no name. Bitcoin doesn't guarantee it: every transaction is public forever on the timechain. With good habits, like new addresses, coin control, running your own node and avoiding KYC, you protect your privacy. Without care, your history can be traced. Privacy is a right, and you have to work for it.

Watching what people do, say or spend. Banks and governments track every card payment; a central bank digital currency would make it total. Bitcoin offers a way out if you look after your privacy: money that doesn't report every purchase to anyone.

Central bank digital currency. It sounds modern, but it's state money where the issuer sees every payment and could block, limit or program it, for example with expiry dates. The digital yuan is an example. It's the opposite of Bitcoin: centralized, surveilled and permissioned.

When a currency is suddenly worth less against others. In Argentina it's a familiar story: your salary buys less from one day to the next. Many people save in bitcoin for exactly this reason: it has a fixed supply and no central bank can decide to dilute it.

The United States currency and the world's main reserve currency. In Argentina it's the classic refuge against the peso, with an official rate and an informal one, the blue. But the dollar is inflationary too, just more slowly, and you depend on banks to hold it. Bitcoin offers a refuge without permission and with a fixed supply.

Money set aside for the future. Inflation eats it slowly; devaluation, all at once. Bitcoin, with its fixed limit of 21 million, is attractive for long-term saving, held in your own custody. It's volatile in the short run, so it's for money you don't need soon.

Money a migrant sends home to their family. Traditional services charge high fees and take days. With bitcoin, and even more with Lightning, it arrives in seconds and costs cents, with no bank in between. For many families it's the most direct use of Bitcoin.

When more people start using something. In Bitcoin, people, shops and even countries taking it up. El Salvador made it legal tender in 2021, a milestone that sparked debate. Real adoption is measured in people who understand it, use it and keep their own keys, not only in headlines.

Trading goods for money. More and more shops accept bitcoin, and with Lightning you pay at the register by scanning a QR in seconds. Every merchant who accepts it makes it more useful as money and less a mere investment: a circular economy, from neighbor to neighbor.

Where people buy and sell and prices are formed. Bitcoin's never closes: it runs 24/7 around the world. Bull market when it rises, bear market when it falls. Bitcoiners know that the price swings a lot, but the rules, the supply and the network keep working the same.

The animal of rising markets, because it charges with its horns upward. A bull run is a long rally, full of euphoria and new arrivals. Bitcoiners enjoy it, but they know the cycles: what counts is not selling in a panic or buying on euphoria, and keeping your keys.

The animal of falling markets, because it swipes downward with its paws. A bear market is the long winter: low prices, little attention and many people giving up. It's also when builders work quietly and when the patient stack sats.

Someone who holds a huge amount of bitcoin. Their moves can shake the price, so many people watch their addresses. Still, no whale can change Bitcoin's rules: the network treats them exactly the same as someone with a few sats.

Earth's natural satellite. 'To the moon!' is the cry when the price shoots up. It's a fun meme, but bitcoiners who stick around know the real goal is not the moon: it's sound money, privacy and freedom.

A token designed to track the value of a currency, usually the dollar, such as USDT or USDC. Useful for avoiding volatility, but there's an issuer that holds the reserves and can freeze your tokens. It's digital dollars with a boss: convenient, but not Bitcoin.

A guardian or keeper. In Bitcoin, whoever holds your keys for you, like an exchange. It's convenient, but you depend on their honesty, their security and the government's permission. Many have frozen or lost their customers' funds. That's why: not your keys, not your coins.

Holding your own keys, with no one else in charge of your bitcoin. It means being your own bank: no one can freeze, seize or lose your coins. It also means responsibility: a good backup of your seed and care. It's the heart of what Bitcoin makes possible.

A tiny payment, of a few sats. With banks it makes no sense because fees eat it; with Lightning it does. You can pay per article, tip a creator or stream sats per minute of a podcast. It opens business models that ordinary money never allowed.

A gathering of people with the same interest. Bitcoin meetups bring local bitcoiners together in a bar, a cafe or a hackerspace to talk, learn and help newcomers. Many learned to take their coins into self-custody at one, with someone patient explaining things in person.

A group that shares something. Bitcoin's is worldwide and has no leader: developers, miners, educators, merchants and plebs who never met. Argentina's is very active, with meetups, conferences and a lot of education. In a network without a boss, community is what sustains it.

The ability to remember. A seed you memorize travels with you even if you lose everything else, which is why some talk about a brain wallet. It's risky as your only backup, since memory fails, but it shows how bitcoin can live in your head and cross any border.

What heirs receive. If no one knows how to access your keys, your bitcoin dies with you. Planning your inheritance, with clear instructions, multisig or timelocks, is part of responsible self-custody: your family should be able to recover the coins without depending on a company.

The ability to bounce back from adversity. Bitcoin has survived bans, crashes, attacks and years of people calling it dead, and it keeps producing blocks. With thousands of nodes worldwide and no center, there's nothing single to knock down.

Something that can't be changed. Once a transaction is buried under enough blocks, rewriting it would cost more energy than anyone could spend. No one can edit the history of the timechain or erase a payment. That's what gives finality to every bitcoin transaction.

Taking no side. Bitcoin is neutral money: it doesn't care about your nationality, ideas or bank. The rules are the same for everyone and no one can exclude you. In a world where money is used as a weapon, that neutrality is worth a lot.

An instrument for telling time. Bitcoin works as a decentralized clock: each block is a tick, roughly every ten minutes, and the timechain records the order of events without anyone in charge. That's why Satoshi called it the timechain.

A person who travels the unknown. In Bitcoin, a website for looking up transactions, blocks and addresses, such as mempool.space. Handy, but every search tells the site what you're interested in; for privacy, run your own explorer on your node.

Tiny leftover amounts. In Bitcoin, outputs so small that spending them costs more in fees than they're worth. Some people send dust to addresses on purpose to track their owners, so many wallets let you freeze it and leave it untouched.

To combine and strengthen. In Bitcoin, merging many small outputs into one, ideally when fees are low, so future spending is cheaper. Careful: consolidating links those outputs together and can reveal that they're yours, so think about your privacy before doing it.

A tag on a product. In a wallet, a note you put on an address or payment to remember where it came from. It helps with coin control: you know which coins came from KYC and which didn't, and you avoid mixing them. Small habit, big privacy gain.

A Bitcoin test network where blocks have to be signed by designated signers. That makes it more predictable than testnet: blocks arrive steadily and there are no chaotic reorgs. Developers use it to try new things without risking real money.

The Onion Router: a network that wraps traffic in layers of encryption and sends it through several relays, so no one sees who talks to whom. Many Bitcoin and Lightning nodes run behind Tor to hide their IP. It's a cheap way to add privacy and censorship resistance.

Software burned into a device. In a hardware wallet it's what protects your keys and signs. Before updating, verify the firmware is authentic: a malicious version could steal your coins. Open source firmware lets anyone check what it does.

Adi Shamir, Israeli cryptographer, the S in RSA. He created Shamir's secret sharing, a scheme to split a secret into parts so that only a certain number of them together can rebuild it. Some wallets use it for seed backups, though many bitcoiners prefer multisig.

Trading one thing for another. In Bitcoin, exchanging funds between networks, for example from on-chain to Lightning, or between two people. It's atomic when either everything completes or nothing happens, so neither side can run off with the other's money without trusting an intermediary.

A vessel that travels underwater. A submarine swap moves funds between the main chain and Lightning without trusting anyone: you send on-chain and get paid on Lightning, or the reverse, tied together by the same secret. Your funds dive into Lightning or come back up to the surface.

The secret whose hash locks a Lightning payment. The recipient knows it and reveals it to collect, and that revelation travels back along the route so each hop collects too. Having the preimage is your proof that you paid: a receipt no one can fake.

A vegetable made of layers. Lightning routes payments in onion style: each hop can only peel its own layer and only knows the previous and next node, not who pays or who receives. Tor works the same way and is named after it. Layers of encryption protecting your privacy.

Something kept back for later. Some people see bitcoin as a long-term reserve of value: scarce, portable and impossible to print. Some governments have discussed or set up bitcoin reserves. For a bitcoiner, the most important reserve is the one in your own custody.

Using borrowed money to bet bigger. It amplifies gains, but also losses: a small dip can liquidate your whole position. Many lost everything trading bitcoin with leverage. Bitcoiners prefer to buy, hold their keys and sleep well.

To use money to pay. In Bitcoin, each output can be spent only once. The double-spend problem, spending the same digital money twice, was what blocked digital cash without a central authority. Bitcoin solved it with proof of work and a public history everyone verifies.

To transmit to everyone. After signing a transaction, your wallet broadcasts it to the network: nodes check it and pass it along until it reaches miners. If you broadcast through your own node, ideally over Tor, you don't reveal to others where it came from.

The name Satoshi gave in early code to what outside Bitcoin everyone calls the blockchain. Many bitcoiners prefer it because it says what it really is: a chain of blocks that orders events in time, with no one in charge, every block signed with work. Bitcoin's public, shared history.

Spread across many places. Bitcoin is distributed over thousands of nodes worldwide, each with a full copy of the timechain. There is no central server: if some go down, the rest keep running. That's why no government or company can turn it off.

The ability to wait calmly. In Bitcoin it's maybe the most important virtue: getting through bear markets, ignoring the noise and thinking in years. Bitcoiners call it low time preference: valuing the future over the urge of the moment.

Someone who uses, studies or builds Bitcoin and believes in what it means: money without a boss, verifiable and with a fixed supply. Plebs, devs, miners, educators: there are many kinds. It's not about the price, but about sovereignty, self-custody and verifying instead of trusting.

Adam Back, British cryptographer who created Hashcash in 1997, a proof-of-work system cited in the Bitcoin whitepaper and the direct ancestor of mining. He was one of the first people Satoshi wrote to. He later co-founded Blockstream, which he leads.

Andreas Antonopoulos, one of Bitcoin's best-known educators. He wrote Mastering Bitcoin, a technical reference many developers learned from, and his talks are collected in The Internet of Money. He explained Bitcoin to the world with a teacher's patience and a defense of open, neutral money.

Wei Dai, computer engineer and cypherpunk who proposed b-money in 1998: anonymous, distributed digital money created through computational work. Satoshi cited it in the whitepaper. His ideas are among the direct ancestors of Bitcoin.

Eric Hughes, mathematician and cypherpunk who co-founded the cypherpunk mailing list and wrote A Cypherpunk's Manifesto in 1993. It says privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age, and that cypherpunks write code. That spirit lives on in Bitcoin.

Tim May, engineer and co-founder of the cypherpunk movement, author of The Crypto Anarchist Manifesto in 1988. He foresaw that cryptography would let people transact and talk beyond the reach of states. Many of his ideas found a home in Bitcoin.

David Chaum, cryptographer and pioneer of digital cash. In the eighties he invented blind signatures, which let you spend digital money without revealing who you are, and he founded DigiCash. It failed because it depended on one company, but his ideas live on in today's ecash, like Cashu and Fedimint.

Gavin Andresen, developer to whom Satoshi handed leadership of the Bitcoin project before stepping away. He created an early faucet that gave away free bitcoins to attract users and helped found the Bitcoin Foundation. He did a lot to grow the early community.

Gregory Maxwell, cryptographer and longtime Bitcoin Core developer. He proposed CoinJoin, to combine payments and gain privacy, and confidential transactions, which hide amounts. He co-founded Blockstream and influenced much of Bitcoin's technical design.

Pieter Wuille, Bitcoin Core developer behind key improvements: he co-authored SegWit and the bech32 address format, and was a lead author of the Schnorr signature and Taproot proposals. He also worked on libsecp256k1, the cryptography library nodes use. Quiet, careful, essential work.

Joseph Poon, co-author with Thaddeus Dryja of the paper that proposed the Lightning Network: payment channels that let you pay fast and cheaply on top of Bitcoin without giving up self-custody. He later co-proposed Plasma, a scaling design for another chain.

Thaddeus Dryja, co-author with Joseph Poon of the Lightning Network paper. At MIT's Digital Currency Initiative he created Utreexo, a design to greatly reduce the storage a full node needs, so more people can verify for themselves.

Michael Saylor, executive who turned his software company MicroStrategy, now called Strategy, into a bitcoin treasury holding hundreds of thousands of coins. Other public companies copied the idea. Known for laser eyes and preaching bitcoin as the best way to store value.

Saifedean Ammous, economist of the Austrian school, author of The Bitcoin Standard, a book that convinced many people of bitcoin as sound money by telling the history of money. He followed it with The Fiat Standard, a critique of today's money.

Jack Dorsey, co-founder of Twitter and founder of Square, renamed Block, which builds Bitcoin products. A committed bitcoiner, he has funded open-source Bitcoin development and Nostr, a decentralized social protocol that resists censorship.

Jameson Lopp, bitcoiner and co-founder of Casa, a company that helps people with multisig self-custody. A go-to voice on security and privacy, he keeps a public list of physical attacks against bitcoin holders as a reminder that keeping quiet is part of security.

Jack Mallers, founder and CEO of Strike, a Lightning-based payments app. In 2021, at a Bitcoin conference, he emotionally announced that El Salvador would make bitcoin legal tender. He champions Lightning for everyday payments and remittances.

Alex Gladstein, of the Human Rights Foundation, where he works on the Oslo Freedom Forum. He tells the stories of people living under dictatorships, inflation and censorship, and shows how Bitcoin gives them a way to save and get paid that the state can't freeze.

First name of Hal Finney, cryptographer and cypherpunk who created reusable proof of work (RPOW). He was the first person besides Satoshi to run Bitcoin, tweeting 'Running bitcoin', and received the first bitcoin transaction in January 2009. A beloved pioneer.

First name of Ralph Merkle, computer scientist and one of the pioneers of public-key cryptography. He invented hash trees, now called Merkle trees, which Bitcoin uses to summarize all of a block's transactions in a single hash. That lets light wallets check a payment without downloading everything.
